title: SQL Essentials
description: Standard SQL and PostgreSQL: joins, NULLs, aggregation, window functions, indexes, and concurrency.

questions.prompt: This query should list employees who have no manager. One row has manager_id NULL, yet the query returns zero rows. Why?

code.source: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE manager_id = NULL;

options.text: NULL must be quoted as a string literal: WHERE manager_id = 'NULL'
manager_id needs a NOT NULL constraint before it can be compared
Comparing with = NULL yields UNKNOWN for every row; use WHERE manager_id IS NULL
Use WHERE manager_id == NULL, since a single = means assignment

questions.explanation: In SQL, any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN (neither true nor false), and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. IS NULL is the predicate for testing missing values; the string 'NULL' is just text.

questions.prompt: customers has 3 rows (Ana, Ben, Cy). orders has 2 rows for Ana and 1 for Ben. What does this query return?

options.text: 4 rows; Cy appears once with o.id NULL
3 rows; Ana's two orders are collapsed into one row
3 rows; Cy is excluded because he has no orders
9 rows; every customer is paired with every order

questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and repeats it once per match: Ana x2, Ben x1, and Cy once with NULLs for the order columns. Excluding Cy is INNER JOIN behavior; 9 rows would be a CROSS JOIN.

questions.prompt: Given this orders table, what does the query return?

code.source:
id | tip
----+------
  1 |   10
  2 | NULL
  3 |   20
  4 | NULL

SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(tip), AVG(tip) FROM orders;

questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows (4); COUNT(tip) and AVG(tip) ignore NULLs, so AVG is (10 + 20) / 2 = 15. If missing tips should count as zero, use AVG(COALESCE(tip, 0)) = 7.5.

questions.prompt: This query should list customers who have placed more than 5 orders, but PostgreSQL rejects it. Which line is wrong?

code.source:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
WHERE COUNT(*) > 5
GROUP BY customer_id;

questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, so aggregates are not allowed there. Filter groups with HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 placed after GROUP BY.

questions.prompt: True or false: a SELECT without ORDER BY on a table with a primary key returns rows sorted by the primary key.
questions.explanation: The SQL standard and PostgreSQL guarantee no row order without ORDER BY; the order can change with updates, parallel or synchronized scans, and plan changes. If order matters, specify ORDER BY.

questions.prompt: This report should list every customer with their 2024 order count, showing 0 for customers with no 2024 orders. Those customers are missing. Which change fixes it?

code.source:
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders_2024
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

options.text: Change COUNT(o.id) to COUNT(*) so that customers without orders are counted as 0
Change the LEFT JOIN to a FULL OUTER JOIN so unmatched rows from both sides are kept
Add OR o.order_date IS NULL to the WHERE clause so unmatched customers pass the filter
Move the date test into the join: ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.order_date >= '2024-01-01'

questions.explanation: The WHERE runs after the join and discards the NULL-extended rows, effectively turning it into an inner join. Putting the condition in ON keeps every customer. Adding OR ... IS NULL rescues customers with no orders at all, but still drops those whose orders are all before 2024.

questions.prompt: This query should find products that have never been sold. It returns zero rows, although several such products exist. order_items.product_id is nullable. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Some order_items rows have product_id NULL, so NOT IN evaluates to UNKNOWN for every product
NOT IN cannot reference a different table unless the two tables are also joined in FROM
The subquery runs once per product row and times out, so PostgreSQL returns an empty set
NOT IN requires the subquery to use SELECT DISTINCT, otherwise duplicates cancel the match

questions.explanation: x NOT IN (..., NULL) can never be TRUE: it is FALSE when x matches and UNKNOWN otherwise. Use NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id), which handles NULLs as intended.

questions.prompt: A leaderboard query adds rank_col using a window function with OVER (ORDER BY score DESC). Which function produced this output?

options.text: RANK()
ROW_NUMBER()
DENSE_RANK()
PERCENT_RANK()

questions.explanation: DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank and leaves no gaps, so Dee is 3. RANK would also tie Ben and Cy at 2 but then skip to 4; ROW_NUMBER never ties; PERCENT_RANK returns fractions between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: Order the clauses of this query by when the database logically evaluates them.

code.source:
SELECT region, SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders JOIN customers ON customers.id = orders.customer_id
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY region
HAVING SUM(total) > 1000
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

questions.explanation: Rows are produced (FROM/JOIN), filtered (WHERE), grouped (GROUP BY), groups filtered (HAVING), output columns computed (SELECT), then sorted (ORDER BY). That is why ORDER BY can use the alias revenue but WHERE and HAVING cannot.

questions.prompt: users has 2 million rows and an index on email, yet this lookup does a sequential scan. Which change lets PostgreSQL use an index for this query?

options.text: Run VACUUM FULL users; so the existing index is rebuilt
CREATE INDEX ON users (LOWER(email));
Add LIMIT 1 so the planner switches to an index scan
CREATE INDEX ON users USING hash (email);

questions.explanation: A B-tree on email stores raw email values, so it cannot answer a predicate on LOWER(email). An expression index on LOWER(email) matches the query exactly (PostgreSQL docs, Indexes on Expressions). A hash index on email has the same mismatch.

questions.prompt: Which queries return each customer who has placed at least one order, exactly once per customer? Select all that apply.

options.text: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c WHERE c.id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
SELECT DISTINCT c.id, c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;

questions.explanation: EXISTS and IN are semi-joins that return each customer at most once, and DISTINCT removes the duplicates a plain JOIN produces. The plain JOIN repeats customers once per order, and the LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL form finds customers with no orders.

questions.prompt: Two withdrawals of 80 run concurrently on an account with balance 100, using this code at PostgreSQL's default READ COMMITTED level. Both succeed and the balance ends at 20. Which change prevents this?

options.text: Add a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint on accounts so that the database rejects an overdraft
Set the isolation level to READ UNCOMMITTED so each transaction sees the other one's update
Add an index on accounts.id so the SELECT finishes faster and the race window disappears
Use one statement, UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 80 WHERE id = 7 AND balance >= 80, and check the row count

questions.explanation: Both transactions read 100 and write an absolute value, a classic lost update. An atomic conditional UPDATE (or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before computing) serializes them: the second sees 20 and updates 0 rows. A CHECK constraint does not help because 20 is a valid balance, and PostgreSQL treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED.

questions.prompt: This feed endpoint gets slow on deep pages, and users see duplicate posts when new posts arrive while they page. Which approach fixes both problems?

code.source:
SELECT id, created_at, title
FROM posts
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 200000;

options.text: Keyset pagination: WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20, with a matching index
Add an index on created_at so that OFFSET can jump straight to row 200,000 without reading the rows before it
Run each page request in a REPEATABLE READ transaction so every page sees a consistent snapshot of posts
Cache SELECT COUNT(*) FROM posts and compute the OFFSET from the cached total instead of from page numbers

questions.explanation: OFFSET still produces and discards every skipped row, and shifts when rows are inserted. Seeking past the last (created_at, id) seen uses an index on (created_at, id) to start right there and is stable under inserts; id breaks ties. Each request gets a new snapshot anyway, so REPEATABLE READ per request does not help.

questions.prompt: orders has 50 million rows spread across thousands of customers. Which single index best supports this frequent query?

code.source:
SELECT id, total, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = $1
  AND created_at >= now() - interval '90 days'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;

options.text: CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at, customer_id);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, created_at);
Two indexes: one on (customer_id) and one on (created_at)
CREATE INDEX ON orders USING hash (customer_id);

questions.explanation: With the equality column first and the range/sort column second, PostgreSQL jumps to the customer, reads created_at in order (scanning backward for DESC), and stops after 10 rows with no sort. Leading with created_at scans all recent orders of every customer; two separate indexes require a bitmap combine plus a sort.

questions.prompt: On PostgreSQL 16, production has several rows with tenant_id = 42 and external_id NULL, which the team believed this constraint prevents. What explains it, and what enforces their intent?

options.text: A composite unique constraint only checks its first column; list external_id first in the constraint instead
The constraint was disabled during a bulk load; run ANALYZE integrations so it is re-validated and enforced
Unique constraints treat NULLs as distinct by default; use UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT or make external_id NOT NULL
The bigserial primary key already makes each row unique, which overrides the composite unique constraint

questions.explanation: Per the SQL standard and PostgreSQL docs, NULL is not equal to NULL, so rows differing only by a NULL do not conflict. PostgreSQL 15+ supports UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (after removing existing duplicates); a NOT NULL column also works if every row has a value.
